utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the Registry, the Office of the Prosecutor. I see the same counsel attending, and for Defence counsel also, more or less the same counsel who are fully represented. We are here today to begin the Defence case in this trial. But before that, as we promised, we have a few matters to clear up after our discussions last week; we have certain matters to address. Some we will be able to decide upon; others will be pending until certain information is obtained. So the first issue we have to address is the calling of Witness AK. The Chamber believes that witnesses do not belong to anyone. The witness has already testified; nevertheless, if he is willing to appear again, the Defence may try to call Witness AK to testify again. The second issue to address: the request of the Radic Defence for the disclosure of medical documents for Witnesses A and F. The Chamber will not order the Prosecutor to carry out any inquiries on behalf of the Defence. The Prosecutor has presented its evidence. If the Defence wishes to go further, it is free to do so. As the Defence knows the identity of the witness and may conduct its own inquiries, in that sense, the request has been rejected. The third issue: the admission of the transcript of the testimony of Witness R in the Tadic case. For a decision to be made on the admission of a transcript from a hearing, the Chamber needs to know whether the witness will be present in the courtroom or not. The first thing to be done, therefore, is for the Defence to contact the witness to ask him whether he is willing to appear on behalf of the Defence. Following the reply, the Defence may submit to us the request together with the necessary information. Therefore, our decision is that the Defence will ask Witness R from the Tadic case to testify in this case. The fourth issue has to do with Rule 94 ter or 92 bis. The new Rule may reduce the possibility for the Defence to tender written evidence. The Defence has expressed the wish to continue under the provisions of Rule 94 ter in this stage. Rule 6 of the Rules envisages that the coming into force of new amendments will be without prejudice to the rights of the accused. Therefore, in order to maintain the principle of the equality of arms, the Chamber decides that the affidavits mentioned by the Defence in their submission will be regulated by the old Rule 94 ter. There are other pending issues; however, the Chamber is not in a position to rule on them at this stage. That applies to the motion on the confidentiality of schedules to the indictment raised by the accused, Mr. Zigic. The Chamber is awaiting the written response of the Prosecutor. Another question has to do with expert witnesses, a motion on behalf of the accused Mr. Radic. It is the opinion that the Prosecutor will consider the suggestion of the Chamber, to respond in writing to the expert findings, and once the Prosecutor takes a position on this, the Chamber will make its ruling. The motion submitted by the Kvocka Defence counsel, the Chamber still needs to see whether the Prosecutor is satisfied by the explanations given by the Defence or whether they maintain their objections. In any event, the Chamber is not familiar with those documents and, therefore, either the documents will be presented in their entirety so that we can have a response from the Prosecutor and their familiarisation with the exhibits, or the Chamber will make a ruling each time a document is tendered. But the Chamber wishes to tell you that we prefer the former solution, that is, the totality of the exhibits to be submitted and a decision to be taken on all of them. That would be the more efficient procedure. Protection measures, a motion submitted by Mr. Kvocka's Defence counsel. The Chamber understands that Mr. Simic has withdrawn his request regarding safe passage. We are waiting for the Kvocka Defence to give additional explanations regarding the identity of the witnesses and the protective measures they require for each of those witnesses. Perhaps it would be easy to do so in writing, and, after that, we will make a ruling. So those are the decisions and clarifications regarding a number of issues which we addressed in the course of our discussions. For the moment, I think that is all. I am going to give the floor to Mr. Krstan Simic to make his opening statement for the Defence of Mr. Kvocka. So, Mr. Krstan Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you. Your Honours, this trial is a trial of an individual, an individual who, doing his job, a job which he chose as his profession, which he loved, he found himself in the midst of the horrors of a terrible war which swept the former territory of SFRY, especially Bosnia-Herzegovina, where many things occurred which are contrary to international customary law and contrary to human and even divine laws, as we are prone to say. Having mentioned the armed conflict, I wish to underline that in our case, we will not go into any details regarding that conflict, because Kvocka, together with the other co-accused, showed that there was, without any doubt, an armed conflict according to the criteria adopted by the Appeals Chamber ruling concerning the interlocutory motion in the Tadic case. The Appeals Chamber, at the time, came to the following conclusion, and I quote: "An armed conflict exists whenever armed force is resorted to between states or continued armed violence between the authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within the boundaries of a single state." Your Honours, in view of the fact that the existence of an armed conflict is a requirement for the implementation of international humanitarian law, we consider this fact to be undisputed, so we will not go into it so as not to waste any time. However, I have to underline that the work of this Tribunal is indeed in the focus of public attention. The general public, legal experts, professionals, historians, sociologists, and other public officers are focusing their interest on it. I think with a certain time distance, the interest in this Tribunal will become even more significant, and its solutions will represent sources of law and an example of the response of the International Community to certain events. The causes of any civil war, no matter how we may describe it, are always deep, complex, permeated with historical elements, affected by the present, and probably affecting certainly the future. Several experts have appeared in this Tribunal, expert witnesses who have discussed these causes. They've presented various assessments in public, and their positions were frequently controversial, contradictory, and I'm quite confident that with a certain time distance, these events will be described also from a slightly different angle, taking into account the extremely complex and complicated causes that brought about the disintegration of a state in which relations, as testified by witnesses, were almost idyllic. People entered into mixed marriages, lived together in harmony, and then suddenly they seemed to have forgotten all that and embarked upon a bloody war which had such dire consequences for all, which, regrettably, is now the object of work of this Tribunal. When I say "regrettably," it is not because I do not think that justice should be served, but regrettably that such events should have occurred at all. As for the causes of the armed conflict, the Defence would like to highlight only two aspects of this highly-complicated issue and no more than that. Bosnia and Herzegovina was a federal unit as a component part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This federal unit, which had a high level of statehood, according to the constitution, there were three constituent state-forming nations throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was promulgated by the constitution. This was asserted by social relationships and provided for by the appropriate legislation. However, it was prior to the outbreak of this horrific war that certain people started fearing that such a war could break out, and an amendment was adopted to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina which envisaged that, at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a federal unit within the SFRY, a commission be set up for national equality of all three nations or ethnic groups. The constitutional principle on which the work of this commission was based was that the commission should be composed of 15 representatives of each of the state-forming nations, that is, the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats; and that within the framework of this commission, certain issues be discussed and, in view of the level of development already attained, these had to be a very limited number of questions that this commission was intending to address with a view to ensuring equality among all three state-forming nations. It was similarly envisaged that the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the legislative body, should pass a law which would regulate the work of this commission and the terms of reference of that commission. The decisions that this commission was to take had to be taken unanimously. The possibility of one nation outvoting another was excluded. This constitutional provision was designed to ensure equality, to prevent what unfortunately did happen from ever happening. Unfortunately, I have to point out that after the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina which were called by politicians and the public in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- even the International Community described them as democratic only because they were multiparty elections for the first time. This was the first time that several parties participated in the elections as opposed to the previous period when there was only one party, which, in fact, ruled the country, the whole of the SFRY. The peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not respond adequately to this challenge and the chance they were offered, with the introduction of a multiparty system, the adoption of a free-market economy, and democratic principles which had already been well-established and which governed the Western world. The nationalist leaders opted for the concept of nationalist political parties. In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, three such parties were formed: First, the HDZ, the Party of the Croatian Democratic Union, composed almost 100 per cent of Croats; the Party of Democratic Action, known as the SDA, whose members were 99.9 per cent Muslims; and the third to be formed was the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, of which 99.9 per cent members were Serbs. These three nationalist parties - national and nationalistic, as I would describe them because subsequent events proved them to be such - in the first stage, formed a coalition amongst themselves. They constituted the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, removing from the scene all those political forces which advocated a multiethnic principle, which advocated economic and democratic programmes rather than nationalist ones. The absolute power after the elections was taken over by the SDA, SDS, and HDZ. There was no place for members of any other party except for those deputies who were elected by the will of the people and who came to parliament but were subjected to insults, outvoting, and the like. Quite naturally, in view of such circumstances, the three concepts of nationalist parties necessarily had to lead to a conflict within the parliament or assembly. The work of the assembly was blocked, and the commission for national equality never, in fact, came into being. It never had a chance of starting to function, to try and establish the principle of equality of the three nations and thus avoid the war. Similarly, the law to regulate the functioning of this commission was never adopted. In view of these divisions, when the media also played their part in spreading hatred, intolerance, and ethnic animosity, this inevitably led Bosnia-Herzegovina into war. The third question that we must highlight for its importance, words said before this Tribunal, was the question of the referendum. Those two issues as well were the generators of war, in the viewpoint of the Defence team of Kvocka. When I say the two, there was the plebiscite of the Serbian people and the referendum of the Croats and Muslims. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The plebiscite of the Serbian people, which was organised under the leadership of the SDS party, had one overriding issue: the question was whether -- the electorate was asked, do they wish to remain within the composition of the former SFRY? That was the sole question that was asked. Most of the Serbian population, following up this question and intimately opting for Yugoslavia as its own state on the one hand and exposed to the impact of the media, and the media was very much present, supported this plebiscite which was organised by the Serbian Democratic Party. There were very few members of other nationalities who went out to vote in the plebiscite. Bosnia opted according to the national criteria. The Serbs became the enemies of the Muslims, the Muslims became the enemies of the Serbs, and so on and so forth, and the structure was splitting at the seams. After that, the power and authority in Sarajevo was -- supported the referendum on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I must say that the first plebiscite itself, which was organised by the Serbs, was led by the SDS but it was unlawful. It was unconstitutional. It was contrary to the constitutional provisions because the constitution decisively regulated the rules for a referendum to be held. At the same time, the second referendum, the other referendum which was organised by the authorities in Sarajevo, in its initial stage, we could say that it was not contrary to the constitution. Voting places were organised, people were able to go out to vote and state their views with respect to the issues posed by the referendum. However, the result of this referendum was the following: Between 63 and 64 per cent of the voters went out to vote on the referendum, of the electorate of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those are official figures. Affirmatively, that is to say, in support of the decision of a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, that 95 per cent of the voters were in favour of this. For the most part, they were Muslims and Croats. If the truth be told, there were some Serbs amongst them as well. However, the constitution resolutely provided for a provision that the referendum decision would be passed if two-thirds of the electorate vote in favour. Two-thirds -- a two-third majority of the electorate is 66.6 per cent of the voters. It is indisputable that only 63 per cent, 63.4 per cent, that is to say, between 63 and 64 per cent of the electorate went out to vote. Therefore, bearing this fact in mind, that is to say that the necessary majority did not go out to vote and give an affirmative answer, this referendum too was deemed unconstitutional. These two decisions, with the existence of the commission for national equality, in the view of the Defence, were practically the basic generators of what was to happen in Bosnia and Herzegovina later on. In order to bear out what I have just said, I must indicate an assessment of the expert commission led by the well-known French Professor of constitutional law, Monsieur Badinter, and in the Yugoslav drama, it was known as the Badinter Commission, which also reviewed the question of this referendum and formulated it. It said that the referendum was probably valid because it represented the will of the majority of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the eve of a bloody war which, unfortunately, marked the end of a millennium, an expert commission was truly not able to -- in the application of a constitutional provision and constitutional right, as the Crown of all legal systems could have given qualifications and say, "Well, I'm a little pregnant and a little not pregnant," as we say. We consider that it was our duty to present these facts so that we can view the case within the context of all these events and assess the roles and positions of the individuals who found themselves in the situation. They didn't know what to do. They didn't understand what was happening, what was going on. Today, Your Honours, we're talking about plans, about goals and objectives. But it was a time of great confusion, a time when nobody knew what was happening, where you were, what was going to happen, who was pulling what strings. Quite simply, it was the eve of a chaotic situation and, in fact, a civil war. That is why we are very often taken aback by the qualifications of what is going on. It's like chess, a game of chess where everybody seems to have his role. Every policeman, every police station suddenly takes on this type of role, as if we're playing a game of chess. Finally, with respect to the relationships that reigned, I should like to present one more view and observation. Unfortunately, in the situation in which they found themselves, the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who quite certainly did not deserve the fate that they were to have, had as their leaders people who were not up to the task. They were not up to the challenges of the situation they were facing. They sought refuge in their own nation and thereby denying other nations, and this brought us into a situation in which we find ourselves today, that the Prosecution has issued indictments against Mr. Milosevic, for example, against Mr. Karadzic, against the leaders, topical leaders of their day of the Serbs in these critical times. And having an insight into the events and into the work of this Tribunal, we are certain that only death prevented Mr. Tudjman, the leader of the Croatian people in these somber times, from finding himself the object, and a vital one at that, of the interests of this Tribunal and its work which is here to mete out justice and give a chance to the peoples of those regions for reconciliation. Similarly, I should like to mention another leader in these dark times, and that man is a Mr. Izetbegovic. Before this Tribunal, we have had the Celebici case, and the public has become informed with Tarcin, Glavice, and Kazani and the reconciliation of these nations, and it expect it. It expects that within the context of all these nationalistic leaders that we view and assess the role that Mr. Izetbegovic played as well. However, that is under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and its Office of the Prosecution. But we, coming from those parts, wished to see all those responsible for the fate that has befallen us be treated on a footing of equality so that we can receive complete answers, because the chance for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Your Honours, to move ahead is found in a sentence uttered by the late Willy Brandt on one occasion, the leader of the Social Democrats in Germany, when he said: "Truth, repentance, and reconciliation." We would like to believe that this Tribunal is functioning and working towards the implementation of those principles. Your Honours, you have before you a man, an ordinary policeman, the policeman of a local village police station. The Prosecution says that he forms part of a joint plan with full knowledge of the goals and objectives and who supports them and who, in embracing those plans and objectives, finds himself along the road of persecuting his colleagues, people he went to school with, people he worked with, until a little while ago, his closest relations, relatives of his wife, his wife being a Muslim, the closest relations of his sisters, both of whom are married to Muslims. And only for that reason, only because he is a policeman, the leader of a patrol. As we say -- there's a word we use in jargon called "prasinar" or the man on the beat, the dust raiser, who happened to find himself in the police station on whose territory somebody happened to decide to form an investigation centre or camp. That is a matter for rhetorics; it doesn't matter which word we use - for the purposes of forming part of the security detail, internal security. Starting out from the principles of individual criminal responsibility, which are proclaimed in the documents that we apply in this court, the Defence believes that we are trying Miroslav Kvocka here and not a policeman as part of the police force, legislation, the army, justice, which were in the process of -- that is to say, Serbs who, in the disintegration of the SFRY, sought for themselves political as well as state solutions. This observation, unfortunately, was presented in his opening address by Mr. Niemann, that this was done by the police, that this was done by the army, so on and so forth. What we want to say is that we believe that it is Miroslav Kvocka who is being tried here. Now, if we accept the concept that we are, in fact, trying the police force, that we are trying the army, that we are trying the justice system, that we are trying the attorneys who, in those somber times, went about their business and many of them signed agreements - people who left exchanged their property for the property of other individuals - then those attorneys would be part of the persecution because they, in going about their business, could have found themselves in the position where somebody would accuse them of signing 200 agreements, for example, or contracts. The agreements/contracts were not the expression of the free will of the people, of those people, in the broader sense of the word, because the reason for their departure was what happened, and what did happen was nothing good. That is why on several occasions we pointed out, with all due respect for our colleagues, our learned colleagues of the Prosecution, that their version of events frequently took on the concept of collective responsibility. Your Honours, between collective responsibility and fascism, we have a very slight difference, a thin line. There's a thin line between the two. The Defence will endeavour to prove that Mr. Kvocka, and Mr. Kvocka alone, should be tried here; that he defends his own innocence. He was not interested in the interests of the Serbian Republic. What he wanted was to -- and when he wants is to defend his honour. That is why we are afraid of delving, in theory, in moving into the realm of a joint plan, which would lead us to the fact that this joint plan was war, and that all of us who were there are part of the plan. That is why I have taken it upon myself to make a joke and tell Mr. Niemann the following: When Mr. Kvocka said that I belonged, from the very beginning, to a political option that was called the Reformists, that I thank him for that and that I hope that Mr. Niemann will not accuse me. It was a joke but a joke which is rather a bitter one. That is why the Defence, in its defence case, will try and focus on all these issues which will provide an answer to what Kvocka did, what the system was like, what kind of system existed in Omarska, and to highlight the issues that we consider to be important for our defence case. Your Honours, within the context of this case and its investigation, we consider to be extremely important how the camp was set up, the structure of the camp, its organisation, the organisation of the camp itself. Because we feel that when we present these questions, we will be able to provide the answer that we are interested in, and that is: What was the leadership structure in the camp itself? I am going to use the methodology of my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, to show the Trial Chamber some of the documents that we're going to use. I would like to tender the following documents. Your Honours, I would follow the same scenario as applied by Mr. Niemann. I do not have to present these documents to you now because they will be presented in the course of the case, or have already been presented; I should just like to say that I have highlighted the portions of those documents. They will all be exhibits, or are already exhibits. So I would like to ask the usher to present the relevant -- to highlight the relevant sections of those documents on the ELMO, please, so that we have them on our screens. Would you place this document on the ELMO, and I will indicate the portions I would like to highlight. Your Honours, it is a coincidence that the first document which, in his opening address, was used by my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, is the exact same document that I wish to present. Your Honours, it is an order from Mr. Simo Drljaca, and it has been classed strictly confidential. The number is 11-12-20; the date is the 31st of May, 1992. Your Honours, in this order, Mr. Drljaca, as the Chief of the Public Security Station and, by virtue of his function, a member of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, orders -- and I underline, he orders, and he is in a position to order, as Chief of the Public Security Station and by virtue of his membership in the Crisis Staff, which emphasises his authority. This Tribunal, in many of the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, has been delving into the question of the real power and position of the Crisis Staff --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you help us, please, regarding this document?

utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to locate it now. If you give me one second, I will locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not going to give you a minute now. You can do it during the break. We can continue and clarify the matter later; is that all right? Ms. Krstan Simic, please continue. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The document I'm referring to and which you will probably analyse carefully during your review contains all the elements. First, who is issuing the order to whom; what is being ordered to anyone in particular. This document contains, Your Honours, even to whom reports are being issued by anyone who is receiving any particular order. And not only that. This order in its last paragraph, also provides, in fact envisages, who is going to supervise what is to be done. This document, as any other document, also indicates at the end the addressees. Page 3, the last page. Delivered to the Crisis Staff, the one which was set up -- the one which set up the Omarska camp; Coordinators of the Security Services, those who under this order were instructed and in charge of investigations, assessing responsibility, and placing people on premises, locations defined by this order. It was strictly defined which locations would be used for accommodation of prisoners. The Security Services Centre Banja Luka, of Prijedor; the Police Chief, the official in charge of police affairs inside the Public Security Station; Security Chiefs; the general manager of the Ljubija iron ore mines; and Files. That means, Your Honours, we will prove through this document that the order makes it clear who was who in the Omarska camp and who was responsible for certain acts, who was able to do what, and who was able to undertake what. At this point, I must point out that paragraph 6 specifically envisages the tasks of the Omarska police station. That means providing security. We will prove that Kvocka - I will take the liberty of saying this on behalf of others - that Kvocka was just a part, just a segment of this Security Service. We must also not forget that according to the rules which prevailed in the police, it is a regular responsibility of the police. Specifically in situations like this, it is the police which provides security because this involves lists. These are regulations envisaged by the rules which apply to the police in such circumstances when a policeman is given a task envisaged by the rules of his service and when he is informed that it is a temporary job, that this investigation centre will be in place for 10 or 15 days, until certain checks are made. And this was testified to by some of the prisoners who had been told in their own words that this would take only a few days, and that is indeed what happened in those first days. People were questioned, released up to the 10th or thereabouts, they went to their homes, and that was the state of affairs and that is what we will prove. Then at some point the situation turned around, but I will speak of that later. Your Honours, about the releases, I have a document which has not been tendered, and if it would be easier for you to follow, I have a copy of this which I can easily make available to the Trial Chamber, and with the help of the usher, I will do so. This is for the Trial Chamber and the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What will be the number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D37/1. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have before you another report, again a report written on the 1st of July, 1992, that is, in the -- well into the existence of the Omarska camp. It is a report to the municipal staff of the Prijedor municipality. It is submitted -- it was submitted by the Chief of the Public Security Station, Mr. Simo Drljaca. In the first line of this report, we read, quote: "Conclusion number 02-111-108/92, by which the release of prisoners is prohibited, is being fully observed." Your Honours, it is obvious that from the establishment of the Omarska camp and the beginning of its operation, certain changes occurred, and those who were in the positions of simple policemen, ordinary policemen, were not informed of these changes. It is obvious from here, from this document, that this release of prisoners was prohibited by the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality and that this decision was to be implemented by the signatory of this document. I must also say that this is the same person to whom under provisions -- under paragraphs 11 and 12 of this order of the 31st of May, 1992, which I had mentioned a minute ago, everyone in the Omarska camp was obliged to report to every 24 hours. So every 24 hours, each segment of the organisation of the Omarska camp was duty-bound to submit a report to Mr. Simo Drljaca. And as you can see from the previous document, he forwarded those reports to the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality. Thus we are trying, and I think we will succeed in our Defence case to prove who was the commander of the Omarska camp. It was not Zeljko Meakic and it was not Miroslav Kvocka, because as you can see, Mr. Meakic, as commander of the police station unit, was duty-bound, as part of his Security Service, to send a report every 24 hours. If the claim of the Prosecution were true, then the reports would be -- would have gone to Mr. Meakic. From what we can see from the documentation we have and which we received from the OTP, and we have to say here, for the benefit of the public and the Trial Chamber, the Defence was not in a position, this team or any other team, I believe, was not in a position to get hold of any document which would help the Defence prove what it had set out to prove. We received the documents which enabled us to create and organise our defence and give adequate answers, responses. To illustrate the situation in the camp and address the issue of who was who there, we must also point out other paragraphs of this document which indicate that the organisation of the camp was strict and tasks and responsibilities were made very clear. It is quite a different issue, Your Honours, whether people really fulfilled those tasks, whether they had the ability to do so in view of all the circumstances which prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the witnesses will testify to that. Your Honours, there is a whole series of documents which we could show and present wherein the man, as we said, and we will try to show that in our Defence case, could decide various things. Within the framework of the Omarska camp, even a cook or a cleaning woman could not have been changed, and even a man doing manual work as part of his work obligation could not have been changed or replaced without the knowledge and consent of Mr. Drljaca. Even such trivialities were within his purview. Even the cook could not be replaced without the name of her replacement being presented to Mr. Drljaca, for him to establish whether she could indeed fulfil this position. We will also prove that the situation was such that Mr. Meakic had to ask for permission to issue permits to various individuals who had business taking them to the camp. Again we are talking about persons who fulfilled their work obligation and did their work, simply. I ask you, Your Honours, is there anywhere in the world a camp commander who had to answer to all and everyone within the camp without having the power to issue a pass to a cleaning woman who was supposed, again on other people's instructions, to come in and clean? I would say not. There have been documents and documents passing through the Office of the Prosecutor, letters, and I would like my colleagues from the Prosecution to corroborate this: Did they find a single document showing that anyone was submitting reports to Mr. Meakic or Mr. Gruban, for instance -- Mr. Kvocka? Have they found a single document - as I said, all the documents we have, we received from them - have they ever found a report by Mr. Kvocka or Mr. Meakic, signed by them in any way, in any capacity? True enough, I have mentioned a document which we'll present in our case where Mr. Meakic requests special passes to be issued so that he can know who is coming in and out, and he signed this document, Police Station Commander, Zeljko Meakic. On the same page, it says: "Passes collected by Zeljko Meakic." The date was 29 June 1992. My learned colleague, in his opening statement, mentioned also the principle allegedly prevailing in the police, according to which it is an organisation where it is strictly regulated who is who, who acts in which way, and who does what. He presented a document in support of this claim, and I will just refer to the same provisions that my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, referred to. This document has not been marked for identification before. Those are conclusions from a meeting of the police force of the 6th of May, 1992, number 11-12. This letter is dated the 11th of May, 1992 for the simple reason that Mr. Drljaca is acquainting his subordinates with what they are expected to do, and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have the number of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It is D38/1. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will point out the relevant provisions of this decision, and those are paragraphs 7 and 8: "To tighten to the limit the relationship senior officer-policeman-worker." Point 8: "All orders are to be acted upon without question. Any refusal to do so will result in the termination of employment or removal from the reserve forces." Mr. Niemann referred specifically to these items, and so do I, but only in the context of that order and all the other documents, which means that the order from the 31st of May, 1992 and all other orders which were issued along the lines superior/subordinate had to be complied with without being questioned. Failure to do so entailed termination of employment or removal. A policeman who was left without his job was left without his salary, without his wartime assignment. He would go back to the Ministry which gave him a new assignment, and that new assignment would mean a front line somewhere, the front where people got killed every day. When a state is disintegrating anywhere in the world, corruption reigns. People gave bribes on a massive scale. People gave bribes in the police in order to be given an assignment in the reserve police force. Such an assignment gave one safety. It was a lot safer than being on the front in Gradacac or anywhere else, because when Omarska was created, at that time people were going to the front line in Gradacac and never returned. After somebody got killed on the front, as you heard from the witnesses, people came into the camp to take revenge.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Krstan Simic, we are going to work until ten past one so that you should know in advance. Roughly until ten past one. You have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just one more sentence regarding the order dated the 31st of May, 1992. On the document that was disclosed to us, we will see and prove that this order, on behalf of the security, was received by Mr. Zeljko Meakic, the Chief of the Omarska Police Station, which was responsible for the security in the camp. Mr. Kvocka saw that order for the first time here in the Detention Unit when this document was disclosed to us. Your Honours, I must refer once again to the words of Mr. Zupljanin, head of the centre of the Security Services, when in the previous document he says, "My word is law. It has to be respected and followed through without question." My learned friend Mr. Niemann referred to this statement in his opening address, and I am referring to it once again myself. This same head of department, within the framework of his authority in the newly-established police force in the territory that had seceded and was under the control of the Bosnian Serbs, issued a decision on the 17th of June, 1992, which we have already tendered as an exhibit in this Trial Chamber, D9/1. Allow me to quote from this decision: "According to the provisions of the decision, on the 1st of April, 1992, until regulations are passed on the internal organisation of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the head of the patrol region of the Centre of Security Services Banja Luka, the Public Security Station Prijedor, Police Station Prijedor," and the last department, the police station department Omarska where Mr. Kvocka is employed. So the head of the Security Centre, who says that his decisions have to be respected and carried out issues a decision saying that Mr. Miroslav Kvocka shall continue to execute the assignments which he had executed on an identical decision from 1990, which has also been admitted into evidence, and later on, as this decision was of a temporary nature, and again in 1993 we have another exhibit that has been tendered, and according to that decision, he's appointed to head of the patrol sector, but in 1993 only for the Prijedor police station. And, Your Honours, you know that Mr. Kvocka was in a humiliating manner suspended, dismissed from Omarska and then brought back again [as interpreted] on the 23rd of June, 1992. Your Honours, we shall show -- I am informed by my co-counsel that in the transcript it says that Mr. Kvocka returned on the 23rd of June. No, he was dismissed, suspended, fired on the 23rd of June, 1992, and we will come back to that later on in this opening statement. Your Honours, we will present evidence to prove, as has already been discussed in these hearings, that within the Omarska camp system there were four segments for security. One was the internal Security Service, and this was a segment of the Omarska police station and within the framework of which he too performed certain duties in a room next to the communications centre that existed there. A second segment of the Security Service was of a temporary nature, and this is the special police from Banja Luka, who were there in the first half of June and which caused many problems. This segment of the Security Service was removed from Omarska in mid-June. I should like to ask Your Honours to look at Exhibit D18/1 which has been admitted into evidence and which is linked to the work of this particular segment of the Security Service. English version is "/A". Your Honours, you have before you a report on events in the Omarska camp. I wish to draw your attention to the author of this report on the situation and problems linked to the activities of this particular Security Services unit. In the right-hand corner it says, at the bottom of the page, it says, "Simo Drljaca." It does not say that this report is submitted by the commander, the warden, or his deputy. A report on the situation, on the problems within the camp is being submitted by that same man to whom everyone is submitting daily reports. We have no doubt that you will study this document carefully, so I wish to highlight only a few sentences which we consider to be important, and I quote: "This is a unit whose members were commanded by Strazivuk, though he was not able to exert any control over the conduct of this unit," which means, Your Honours, that this segment of the Security Service was under the command of Strazivuk and not the commander of the police station department Omarska, that is, Mr. Zeljko Meakic, not to mention any one of those here present, any one of the accused. In order to corroborate our submission, allow me to quote the last sentence of this document: "That the allegations in this report are true can be confirmed by all the operatives and the team of experts headed by Mirko Jesic and Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic." Your Honours, the indictment says that Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Meakic were the commanders, then deputies, then we don't know what, we won't know when, and from where and until when. On the 13th of June, however, when Omarska was operational, when things started to happen once release was prohibited, this report is not being submitted by any one of them; far from it. They are so insignificant. The commander of the police station department is so insignificant that Mr. Drljaca doesn't even find it necessary to mention him as a person whom may provide information such as is contained in this letter. His significance is such that Mr. Meakic is not even mentioned as one of the people who can confirm this. This was a department of the Omarska police station, a department that is at the lowest level in the hierarchy, which has such authority, as we will describe in the presentation of evidence, that a Chief of the Security Centre, knowing that it has no significance, that is, that Mr. Meakic has no significance, doesn't even mention him as a person whose authority could confirm to the superior that members of another unit are causing problems within the security service, and this is causing certain conflicts with members of the security as a whole. Your Honours, we will set out to prove that the bishop of Banja Luka, a person who proved to be, in this war, a highly humane person - Dr. Franjo Komarica was his name - wrote a letter and made a plea and sought assistance for the release of the detained priest, Stipo Sosic. Your Honours, that letter was not addressed to Mr. Meakic, the Commander of the Omarska Police Station Department, but again it was addressed to that same person who is the author of all reports and who is the recipient of all the reports relative to the Omarska camp. Finally, Your Honours, when the media showed interest in the events in the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps, when public interest was aroused and when certain reports on the real state of affairs reached the leadership of the Security Services Centre, I wish to indicate that the head of that centre, on the 14th of August, 1992, set up a commission consisting of Vojin Bera, as the president of the commission; Vaso Skondric, as member; Ranko Mijic, member; and Jugoslav Rodic, member, and instructed them, within a time period of three days, to go on the spot to investigate and establish the facts linked not only to events in the Omarska camp, as well as Keraterm and Trnopolje, but also in the territory of the Public Security Stations of Sanski Most, Novi Grad or Bosanski Novi, which were also under the jurisdiction of the Public Security Station. With the help of the usher, I should like to distribute copies of this report because we believe that, with the help of that report, we will be able to draw attention to certain relevant facts. This is a document, too, that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor in the process of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, I have a document here with me bearing the number D38/1. It is the document dated the 11th of May, 1992. What are we going to do with that, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was already previously submitted. If you'd like me to go through the numbers of all the exhibits thus far, I can. We have four exhibits and some of them were tendered already, which I've identified the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take care of this because there is a risk that we may have different numbers for the same document. We have to be very careful about this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. I've met with both the Defence and the Prosecution during the break and we've sorted out the numbers, and we can do this perhaps after the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Shall we call it D38/1 bis now for the sake of continuing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You see, Madam Registrar, the confusion we are in. We have to clarify this once and for all. So this document, dated the 11th of May, 1992, you're telling us that the document has already been tendered. What is the number of that document, or what was the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number of the document was D38/1, but we realised that there was an error and it is now D37/1. This document that they've just tendered is now D38/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So my question is: The document distributed today with the number D37/1, dated the 1st of June, 1992, what is its number now, which had the number D38/1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 1st of July, you mean?
