utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That has already been submitted and that is D20/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document we have before us now, the report, it is D38/1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I really think that either the counsel or the Registry must take care to avoid such situations in the future; otherwise, we will be wasting a lot of time. What is worse, when we start our review, we won't know what we're talking about, we will not be able to understand one another. We have to be very clear with the markings, please. So, Mr. Krstan Simic, you may continue. The number of this document now is D38/1. Thank you very much, and please continue. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Bearing in mind the extent and content of this report, I have no doubt that Your Honours will review this report in its entirety, because it really will be of assistance in gaining a global idea of the situation in the region around Prijedor. However, for the purpose of this opening statement, I just wish to draw your attention to certain parts as an illustration of what I'm talking about in this part of my statement. On page 3 of both the Serbian and the English version, you'll find the following words, and I quote: "On the 27th of May, 1992, further to a decision --" I'm sorry, it is the fourth page of the English version. I will start from the beginning. It is the last paragraph on page 4: "On the 27th of May, 1992, pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, all the prisoners from the Keraterm facility in Prijedor were transferred to the facility in Omarska. "Pursuant to the same decision, the Omarska facility was placed under the direct supervision of the police and the army. The police, that is, the Omarska Police Station, was charged with the immediate security of the facility, of the administration building itself, the workshops, and the garages for the work machinery, while the army took over in-depth security in the form of sentry posts and the mining of certain areas as they saw fit." Your Honours, this report also confirms that the Police Station Department of Omarska had a classical police role envisaged by the rules of service of the police, that is, to provide security, the so-called internal security, of the buildings and facilities listed here. Your Honours, on page 8 or, rather, page 11 of the English version, where this report analyses the situation of collection centres within the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most, which borders on Prijedor municipality, in the first paragraph which addresses events Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. within the territory of Sanski Most, it says, and I quote the last sentence of the first paragraph, I quote: "As a result of a special decision of the Crisis Staff, a prison was set up in the Betonirka facility. A warden and assistant warden were appointed and police employees were engaged in security matters together with members of the army." Your Honours, this is a comprehensive report, and if indeed there had been a warden of the camp or the prison or the collection centre in Omarska, then this report would reveal it in the same way that it revealed that such a warden existed in the mentioned prison in Sanski Most. With the help of all these documents, we wished to show that Mr. Kvocka, head of the regional patrol sector, in accordance with the decision of the 17th of June, could not have been the warden because there is not a single document of any relevance for this period that would indicate that. Your Honours, to round off this question of the organisation and structure of the Omarska camp, allow me to refer to another document. It is the decision dated the 22nd of June -- no. I'm sorry. I apologise. I beg your pardon. I do apologise. There seems to be a misunderstanding. Anyway, it's a decision on the release of persons from detention, dated the 2nd of June, 1992, which we will tender into evidence, where it explicitly says, and I quote: "Personally responsible is the chief of the security station who alone, by his signature, can release a detained person." So the chief of the security centre can alone, by his signature, release any person detained in Omarska or Keraterm. Your Honour, there's no need for me to remind you that that is that same person to whom all reports are addressed, that all have to account to with respect to Omarska camp. You will see that in the report that we have just been reviewing. After the camp was disbanded, it was precisely Mr. Simo Drljaca who submitted his part of the report where, following orders of the head of the Security Services Centre, submits a report. Why? The answer is a simple one; because he's the only person who had the authority to decide about everything happening in Omarska. He was the only person who had the authority to have the necessary information, the only one who could release detainees, the only one who dared submit reports about this to anyone. Thereby, Your Honours, this completes this part of my statement relevant to the organisational structure, which will be a very important element of the presentation of evidence during the Kvocka case in an effort to show that Kvocka did not have any authority beyond the official authority stemming from his job, and as a consequence of his activities, he was expelled from Omarska. Your Honours, the -- following your request for the Defence of the 15th of December, 2000, for motion for acquittal, the Defence will deal with the time period which Mr. Kvocka spent in Omarska. We consider that he can only be responsible, if it were to be established that he was responsible, for that time that he spent in Omarska. The Defence will prove that Kvocka was in Omarska from the 29th of May to the 23rd of June, 1992. True, Mr. Kvocka, after being suspended or released, and he's not quite clear on what it meant on the 23rd, until he returned to the reserve police station, to which he returned on the 1st of July, 1992, it meant that he visited his relations two or three times in Omarska, his brother's relations, in-laws, brothers-in-law, but he did not work there. He went there to visit his brothers-in-law, to take them parcels as he used to do every day. As Witness F said, he would bring parcels in every day. So it is not strange that he came in two or three times after he was released from the camp. But the last time that he was in Omarska was on the 2nd of July, and we are going to prove that because he remembers that particular day. And after that, because of the relationships and tension that were linked to his name, his conduct, his marriage, he did not go to visit there anymore. Quite simply, he was no longer able to take his brothers-in-law any change of clothing or food because he was afraid for his own security and safety, and many witnesses will testify to that. So in that period from the 29th of May to the 23rd of June, Mr. Kvocka, on two occasions, was absent. The first time, for two or three days after the shooting that we're going to talk about on the 30th the of May, because it is quite understandable, in view of the situation he was in, he was under stress, and so Mr. Meakic, his leader, let him leave for a few days, have a few days off. And as Mr. Radic said in his interview to the Prosecution, "What could I have done? Mr. Kvocka could have been killed." And for that he could give two days leave as remuneration. Kvocka, on another occasion, was absent from the camp for health reasons towards the end of his stay there, and also for professional reasons, because at the time, sometime around the 12th or 13th [as interpreted], Strahilo Popovic was killed, who was a member of the reserve police force. And Mr. Kvocka, in the course of May, while he was going about his regular duties, took away some money from the wife of the said Popovic because it was thought that she had engaged -- it was alleged that she had engaged in the trafficking of foreign exchange. Your Honours, by confiscating that foreign currency -- when he confiscated the foreign currency, he issued an official certificate because it was within the scope of his regular official duties, and we shall tender evidence to that effect. After the killing of this individual, Mr. Meakic told Mr. Kvocka that bearing in mind the times they were living in and bearing in mind the expenses incurred for the funeral, that the confiscated money should be returned to the widow of the late Popovic. My assistant has indicated that in the transcript, when we spoke of the killing of Strahilo Popovic, only the days were entered. It was the 12th -- around the 12th and 13th of June, 1992. That is the date, to avoid any misunderstanding. So it was not the relevant time when Mr. Kvocka was in Omarska. It was in the relevant time when Mr. Kvocka was in Omarska. I apologise. Your Honour, the indictment charging Mr. Kvocka charges him with serious crimes, crimes for which you must prove intent. In this opening statement, we are not going to deal with legal issues because legal issues will come later on, once we have presented all the relevant evidence and once we hear all the evidence put forward, but we would like to say a few words about intent, the issue of intent. Stemming from -- starting out from Mr. Kvocka, Mr. Kvocka comes from a poor family with five children. There was -- his father was a physical labourer in the firm of Zitoprodukt Prijedor, where he worked as a porter and loader. The family frequently had to contend with the problem of hunger. Once he completed his primary school, Mr. Kvocka selected the school for internal affairs for two reasons. One reason was that he liked being a policeman; and second, perhaps the more important reason, was that that education was free. It afforded accommodation, free accommodation in a dormitory, uniforms were issued, and the most important thing, once he had graduated from that school which was in Sarajevo at Vrace, he was assured of getting a job and a salary with it, and that meant one less mouth to feed in the Kvocka family. He attended school, and the first group of witnesses will testify to that, that testifies an ambitious man. His ambition was to become a good policeman, and his childhood friend will bear that out. He graduated as one of the best in his class. That means to say he was amongst the first ten, the best ten, which meant that he received an award and the privilege of choosing his place of employment. He chose and he went to work in Prijedor. The school for internal affairs in Sarajevo is a multi-ethnic school. In the police force, there was a rule, that is to say that each nation and nationality should be equally represented. And when I spoke about the commission, I don't want you to gain the impression that there was inequality. It was a school which nurtured a spirit of brotherhood and equality, a spirit of partnership, because we all know that being a policeman means -- is a dangerous profession, and you have to work with your partner. You have to have a partner and a colleague you can rely on at all times, and it doesn't matter whether your partner is a Croat, a Muslim, or some other nationality or ethnic group. What is important is that you can rely on him. And that is why that subject was nurtured in the school and special attention was given to this equal representation. Brought up in the spirit of equality of that kind, he went to Prijedor, he formed a family, he married, and his wife was a woman from an old Muslim family. The Omarska region, ethnically speaking, is a Serbian region with a very marked tradition, but that did not stop Mr. Kvocka or his family from embracing their daughter-in-law who was a Muslim. During Mr. Kvocka's assignment - on one occasion he was sent to France where he provided security detail for the SFRY embassy - she lived in Omarska. His wife lived in her in-law's house and she travelled by train every day to Prijedor, going to work and coming back from work. Mr. Kvocka's spirit and relationship towards his marriage and his family was echoed by other family members. His sisters also married Muslim men. Unfortunately, the war brought with it tragedies, and a particular tragedy for his two sisters. One lived with her Muslim husband in Stolac, in Capljina. With the persecution that existed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, she was expelled and today lives in the United States of America. Her mother and father have not seen her for ten years. It was difficult when his parents were not able to see their daughter. As for his other sister, she was divorced. But since Mr. Kvocka's trial, to the present day, I can inform the Trial Chamber of another tragic occurrence. It concerns Kvocka's other brother-in-law who worked on construction machinery and whose body was excavated from a mass grave in Bosnia. So the child of Kvocka's sister is an orphan, without a father. Once again, did Kvocka really want to leave his little nephew without a father? Your Honours, we are going to prove that Mr. Kvocka, and I quoted Witness F a moment ago, Mr. Kvocka brought parcels to Omarska every day, helping people, helping them to survive, to soften the fate that they experienced in Omarska. Your Honours, we are going to show that Mr. Kvocka, on the 30th of May, in front of a drunken man who had allegedly lost a brother, stood in front of the barrel of a rifle to protect the Muslims. Unfortunately, two or three of them were killed on the occasion. Some were wounded and have survived, and we expect to see them before this Tribunal, we expect to see them come to court. The man was so beside himself on the occasion that when he shot out, he hit a member of the reserve police department, Miroslav Nisic, whose affidavit we have. We also have eyewitnesses of that tragic event. We ask again, and we shall show, a man who has intent to persecute, kill, torture, and rape someone, if he puts his life at risk to protect those who would have been killed, then he cannot be guilty of intent. Your Honours, that would be an absurdity. The days off that he was given - Mr. Radic said they came as a reward to Mr. Kvocka - Mr. Kvocka used those days to see what happened to other members of his family, to his friends, the Muslims. In his apartment at Pecani, he found several elderly Muslim women and he gave them food during the days that he was off duty. Your Honours, amongst those women was the mother of Emir Beganovic, who was the first witness to testify before this Tribunal. Mr. Kvocka took out food from Omarska because Emir Beganovic's mother was a friend of Mr. Kvocka's mother-in-law. There were five or six other women in his flat at the time and they took advantage of the fact that Mr. Kvocka was a policeman. They found safety and security in residing in his apartment. Many witnesses will testify to that, and brothers-in-law as well, as well as the wife of Mr. Kvocka, who has lived through all those difficult times and has emerged. Your Honours, could a man have taken part in persecution who was expelled from Omarska? And the guards laughed when this happened. I apologise to the ladies because I'm going to use bad language. The man who sent him off said, "Kvocka, take down your pants to see if the Muslims circumcised you when they sucked out your brain." Because of relationships of this kind, Kvocka was the target of extremists, he was the target of threats. Mr. Radovan Daljevic, a teacher by profession whose professional options took him to the police force, and whose affidavit we have, says in one section, "It is really astonishing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that Mr. Kvocka survived those times at all." But he survived and he is here today. We are going to prove that Mr. Kvocka was not a member of a political option of any kind, the political option which focused on nationalistic issues. Mr. Kvocka was the member of an idea which was called the Reformist Alliance. It was Yugoslavia's last chance. He tried to do some work within that alliance but, unfortunately, that idea was overthrown. He was never a member of the SDS. His conduct, his actions, and the questions he dealt with, what he strove to achieve, his relationship towards multiethnicity, were demonstrated later on. Mr. Kvocka, in 1994, and that was a war year - contrary to the paragraphs which we adopted as indisputable fact, 343 and 345, which testify to mixed marriages and where words were uttered which are difficult to utter before this Tribunal - he was a kum to mixed marriages, best man to mixed marriages. In fact, he married a Muslim. So he followed his ideals, the ideals of equality and not persecution - equality. He was kum, and in the area that I come from, by being kum, you become a family member, and customary law prohibits kums from entering into marriage. Your Honours, it was no formal undertaking, the undertaking of a kumship. It was an affair that was celebrated in Mr. Kvocka's apartment. He found jobs for his fellow kums. He would beg people to find his own kum a job, who was an electrician. He was a Muslim electrician and nobody wanted to employ him. Nobody wanted to employ Serb electricians either, but especially not Muslim electricians. But he managed to find a job for his kum in order to help the man survive. People who knew Kvocka were ready to give jobs to his friends, despite the fact that they were afraid for their families in doing so. As I say, they were, indeed, troubled times, and we will show how far he went to find jobs for Muslims in that terrible year of 1994. This story about multiethnicity and Kvocka's attitude towards other ethnic groups, towards other nations, let me say that while Kvocka was in the Detention Centre here, his daughter married and he has gained a grandchild. She married a Croat. So that now, today, the fan of this -- the circle has come full circle. The Kvocka family has members belonging to all three ethnic groups. Now, I ask you, a man whose wife is a Muslim, whose sisters are married to Muslims and whose daughter has married a Croat, who has been kum to Muslim families, is that man ready to persecute, to annihilate? No, Your Honours, he is not. If we analyse the documents with all due care and attention, then we could have had a different indictment and taken a different position. His life convictions, his professional options did not fit in with the official policies very well, even at that time. I would now like to point out to you a document which has not been tendered. So I kindly ask the usher ... I would like you to take this document into account, that is, decision 03-531/92, of the 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D39/1. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this decision speaks of suitability. It deals with what kind of people are suitable for certain positions. In paragraph 2 of this decision, we read: "Also, in these positions, we cannot have members of the Serbian ethnic group which have not confirmed their convictions in the plebiscite. The only real official representative of the Serbian people is the Serbian Democratic Party." Obviously, Mr. Kvocka, fortunately for him and his conscience, did not satisfy this criterion. That this is true is confirmed by the following: In August 1992 - I will not burden you with any documents - companies, squads, platoons, police organisations of Prijedor were established. There were about 56 commanders appointed in the process or thereabouts. Among those 56 people, Miroslav Kvocka was nowhere. And about 180 policemen were in engaged, employed in the police station in 1992. That means that every third man was commander of a platoon, a company, a squad. We will show this through evidence. And Miroslav Kvocka is nowhere among them. Your Honours, this is a case about tragic events, events involving people, some of whom who have survived. Talking to one witness who spent in Omarska almost the entire time since its establishment to its dissolution, I heard him saying at one point, "Omarska was an evil in itself." However, the people who come before this Tribunal, the people who come before the public, when they speak about Omarska, they tend to mix reality with stories they heard from other people and help create and add to the confusion that exists about Omarska already, which is certainly unnecessary because Omarska was an evil in itself. I draw your attention to the words of this man because that is a man who carries great pain in his heart because of his experience there, but he has no hatred, and his words echo the words of one witness who appeared here. I am not now looking at the transcript, I am trying to quote her from my memory. Judge Riad asked her when she went to a third country, did she hear from anyone who had been at Omarska stories or the real truth about the fate of her husband who, unfortunately, was one of its victims. She answered that when she arrived in the third country in question, she met at least 50 people who introduced themselves as eyewitnesses of the event, the death of her husband, and that everyone described it in a different way. All the eyewitnesses described the event differently, and she did not want to draw any conclusions from their stories about how her husband died, and she wanted to leave it to the Trial Chamber to establish how it really happened. What I quoted from the words of these witnesses show in the best way how many contradictory statements we hear about events which have been witnessed by many, memories and realities and statements get mixed up. One of the witnesses who testified in public said he saw little. People who testified to only what they have seen really testify to only a little. Somebody who is in a closed room and left the room only for about 40 minutes at a time for lunch, for instance, could not have seen very much. Without avoiding the legal truths, we should strive to establish the real truth, and if we succeed in this, I hope we will be able to prove that Mr. Kvocka did not do anything, that he was not part of any plan, he did not support any plan. He simply was a victim of the events which fell upon many towns and places in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which took many lives. Our job here is to tell the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. We had envisaged a break for ten past one, but I think this is a good moment to stop. So that means that we shall adjourn now for 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence calls its first witness, Zdravko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Judge is addressing you, the Presiding Judge. You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I understand that your name is Zdravko Samardzija; I'm sure I'm not pronouncing it right. You are now going to answer questions which will be put to you by Defence counsel, Mr. Krstan Simic, after which there will be questions from the Prosecutor and possibly by the Judges. Thank you for coming. Mr. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you, Mr. Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We know each other well. We have discussed these questions at length, and also with my investigators you have had contacts, so we'll be talking about those things here. As the proceedings are being simultaneously interpreted, I have been warned by them repeatedly to slow down so it was my turn to remind you to make a pause between the questions and answers so that they don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: For the record, will you tell Their Honours your name.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: My name is Zdravko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. I see that Ms. Susan Somers has something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to just ask the Chamber if it is aware that there appear to be notes of some kind in front of the witness. I do not know what they are, but there are some notes that are being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, [In English] do you know if the witness has some notes or something like this? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the conversations that Mr. Samardzija and I myself had, he took a few notes on a piece of paper, just an outline, which he can show to everyone, which will speed up this discussion regarding the organisation of the Security Service. If the Prosecutor objects, there is no need for us to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, [In English] would you like to see the notes, to have a look? If it's to speed, it's a very good idea, but I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it is to speed, perhaps. If it is to substitute for independent recollection, which would be a concern, then I would ask the Court, perhaps, to have a look itself before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We've had experiences with some witnesses who did have some notes here, and I think it's been held to be sufficient that if you want to see the notes, you have a right to see them, but if it's not a text that he's reading from, which it obviously isn't, other witnesses have been allowed to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If that's the practice in this Chamber, then I'll certainly defer to it. I would ask then either to see them now or to have a copy perhaps made available for me. Thank you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Please have a look immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would have no objection. If we may have a copy of this after the witness finishes testifying, we would be very grateful for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] You will receive a copy immediately after this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much. You may continue, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let us continue, Mr. Samardzija. Would you tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Zdravko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of February, 1954, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where are you residing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I'm living in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Since 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What schools did you attend and graduate from, if any?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I graduated from secondary administrative school and the Faculty of Law in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Have you done your military service?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: In Bileca, the reserve officer school. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you finished your military service, did you acquire any rank?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you completed your education, where did you find employment?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Upon the completion of my education, I was employed by the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is your status now?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I am a pensioner just now. I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So you spent your whole working life working within the police of the SFRY and later of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you employed, in which town?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I worked throughout in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your previous answer, you mentioned that you were working in the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. Could you tell us what that Security Service Centre represents?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The Security Services Centre, in organisational terms, comes second to the Ministry of the Interior, and it consists of two departments; one is the Public Security Department and the other is the State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So you worked in the State Security Department. All the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, let us try and define the chain of command in the centre. The head of the State Security Service in the centre, who was he subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: He was subordinate to the head of the centre, but he was also linked to the under-secretary for state security who was based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does that mean that some reports from the State Security Department could be addressed higher up to the MUP, bypassing the head of the centre of the Security Services?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The State Security Department had its own chain of command so that it could, independently of the Security Services Centre, communicate, though this was rarely resorted to. In principle, all documents went through the regular system of communication. This means that the head of the Security Services Centre could have insight into all the activities of the State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, what was the duty of the State Security Department within the police system of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: It was twofold. We had one set of assignments strictly specified by our rules of service, and we also had the obligation to provide professional assistance to the Public Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned the other department within the framework of the Security Services Centre, that is, the Department for Public Security. What were its duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The Public Security Department had obligations specified by law, which again consisted of several sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What sections were they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: They were sections for the general police, the traffic police, the crime sector which was again subdivided. Then there was the personnel sector, the financial sector, the sector for passports and aliens, and I can't remember whether there were any others, though I think I have covered them all. And also, I'm sorry, the sector for defensive preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who headed the centre, Mr. Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The head of the centre who was in charge of both departments. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, as our aim is not to analyse in detail the organisation for Their Honours, but you said that this was second in the hierarchy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was the third level?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The third level were the public security stations, and the fourth level were the public security station departments. That was the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within the framework of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, were there departments?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were police station departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: No, no, I'm talking about the CSB, the centre. Were there public security stations? That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you remember how many security stations were part of the system that came under the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: There were three public security stations and there was a department for covering trains. And, I'm sorry, there were also village departments. So, you see, that is the fourth level that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Banja Luka have its own public security station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Banja Luka had.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Prijedor have its own public security station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who headed the public security station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The head and assistant head were in charge of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How was the public security station subdivided, if you know? Did it have any subsections?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The public security station had its own subdivisions, so that there was the general police and the traffic police within the framework of the public security station; and then also there were patrolled regions in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there a crime police sector?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there a sector for economic crime?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, the same as in the centre, the difference being that there were fewer officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So there was the public security centre, and the public security station was similar in organisation.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The names were the same, only the number of staff differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within the framework of the public security station, were there police officers in uniform, and how were they called?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were men in uniform. They were called militiamen in those days or policemen. And also their superiors in uniform, it was clearly designated where the superiors wore uniforms and where they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within the framework of the public security station, was there a police station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within the police station or militia, as they were called, were people in uniform employed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who headed the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Heading the police station was the commander, his deputy, and his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who represented the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The police station commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there any possibility within the framework of police stations, in view of the territory they covered, could police station departments be organised?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In what cases did this occur?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Such police station departments or outposts were formed in more remote areas, in localities that were no longer towns but were considered villages or rural areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: These police station departments, did they have their headquarters or buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know, these police station departments, how they were staffed, who headed them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Heading the police station department was the commander of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did those police station departments have deputy commanders or assistants, as was the case in police stations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: No, they only had a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many policemen would there be in such police station departments?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: These were small police stations and the number of staff was adjusted to the area covered, which were usually remote villages, and these were known as patrol sectors, as opposed to municipal police stations where they were, again, subdivided into precincts.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, let us now focus on the reason we brought you here, and that is the year 1992. In those days, you were working in the State Security Sector of the Public Security Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was your position?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I was working in the fifth sector as an instructor for communications and encryption. That wasn't the name it was given --

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Did you later become the head of that department?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In 1992, when ethnic tensions were running high, when incidents were frequent, were you given a different assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I was given the assignment to be a liaison officer with the United Nations and international organisations in view of the fact that I spoke English. I received those instructions from the head of the centre of the Security Service, who designated me as one of those liaison officers. There were several of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, as part of your duties, did you go to the territory of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In that capacity as liaison officer with representatives of international humanitarian organisations, in 1992, after the disbanding of camps, did you take these men to Trnopolje and Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, through your contacts, did you come to know a person called Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca was appointed head of the Prijedor police after the events that occurred in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was that after the takeover of authority by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet Simo Drljaca on a number of occasions actually?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As a person with a lot of experience in police work, how would you briefly describe him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Very briefly, he was not a professional. He lacked police knowledge and this showed in his conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How did he behave, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: He engaged in official interviews outside official premises, which is quite unusual under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How did he dress in public?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I noticed that he would wear white Adidas sports shoes, which was quite unusual for a man of his position. Actually, that is how he seemed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards people? Was he tolerant? Could you describe him in that sense?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: In my assessment, he was a man who was rather crude in his behaviour and this was a reflection of his character.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned these interviews or contacts with him outside official premises, the police, or others. On one such occasion, since you were working in 05 sector, did Mr. Drljaca make certain requests of you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. He requested from me that I operatively covered. That is how it was called officially, but it really meant that I -- that I listen in on certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is the official designation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Operative technical cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Operative technical cover. What does that mean? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: It means the use of all measures at the disposal of state security services to establish certain facts relating to a particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did that imply tapping somebody's conversations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did you have this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: In the Sokolski centre or sports centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In what town is that centre situated?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: It is situated in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is, the Sokolski centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The Sokolski centre consists of a gymnasium, that is, a sports hall; several auxiliary halls; and a kind of cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How was Mr. Drljaca dressed on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I think he was wearing sports clothes, casual clothes. I can't remember exactly what it was he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said that he asked you to eavesdrop on certain people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he tell you what the purpose of that tapping was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: He said that within the territory of the municipality there were a large number of unreliable Serbs, and his explanation for this request was that he wanted to get evidence about their unreliability. That was the gist of his explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, can you remember any of the names of the people that Mr. Drljaca wanted you to listen in on?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact names, but I remember the surnames. He mentioned Kvocka and Simo Miskic. I know his full name because I knew him as a policeman and I was surprised. Mr. Kvocka also, and three other men whose names I cannot recollect now, but I think his request referred to three or four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he mention the name of Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I don't think he mentioned both those names, so I can't actually say, but I can say with certainty that Mr. Simo Miskic, about Simo Miskic and Mr. Kvocka, because I remember hearing that because of the specific surnames and their meaning. Kvocka, of course, means a hen, so I remembered that name. Otherwise, I didn't pay too much attention to the names. And I informed my superiors about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, on that occasion, did Mr. Drljaca explain why for all the names that he mentioned? Did he mention the reason that you had to intercept their conversations or was the reason a general one?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Well, yes, he gave me a general reason and said that they were people whom he -- whom he thought were unreliable and had reason to doubt, suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you answer Mr. Drljaca back, in view of his rank?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I told him that it wasn't in my competence to deal with matters of this kind and that it was the heads of departments whose job it is to make decisions of that kind and that he should contact those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you informed your superior about the conversation.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The rules of service make it incumbent upon me to do so, to convey things of this kind to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I know that a lot of time has gone by, but do you perhaps recall when approximately you had this conversation in the Sokolski centre between you and Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: It was sometime in 1992. I would say mid-1992, which would make it mid-June, perhaps, or the beginning of July. But it was probably in the first few days of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you worked in that department, as you said, for monitoring or eavesdropping on citizens, did you get any subsequent information about similar requests made by Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: When this occurred, I wasn't actually working on jobs of that kind, but quite naturally, while having a cup of coffee perhaps with my colleagues, I did hear that there was a rather lengthy request made, which I'm not sure was complied with because I don't think the technical possibilities existed, and I think the explanation was that he didn't bear the technical feasibility of this in mind when he made his requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You don't know Mr. Kvocka personally, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You have never communicated with him, never seen him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: No. I have never seen him. I don't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers. I see that Mr. Simic is posing a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that at this point we get away from the leading nature of the initial inquiry and that the witness recall from his own memory, not that he have the testimony of Mr. Simic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure you agree, Mr. Krstan Simic, don't you? There we have it. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think these were leading questions, and you know the method of preparation. We discussed these questions at length last night and generally, but I will try to abide by what Ms. Somers has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps we should meet these standards. Please go to the core of the matter, the heart of the matter, because I think that we will agree that if we're not -- when we're not going to the heart of the matter, we can guide the witness a little bit. But I would like to ask you, Mr. Krstan Simic, to proceed in a somewhat different way at present. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. I, of course, accept your proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, I would now like to move on to another area. Did you hear when the Keraterm and Omarska camps were disbanded?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any information with regard to the fact that after the events that occurred in the camps became known, a certain commission was set up in the CSB, the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who founded the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: After the irregularities that were found to have existed, the head of the Security Service set up the commission. Mr. Stojan Zupljanin was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The State Security Sector, was it supposed to provide a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, the composition of the commission was to be a mixed one.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who represented the State Security Sector in the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I think that it was the head at the time, Mr. Vojin Bera. And there was someone from the Prijedor detachment, I think, but I'm not quite sure who that was. I also know some of the members of the commission from the Public Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I know that they were Vaso Skondric, and I also know that Mr. Vaso Skondric was there when -- he was also a member of the commission together with Mr. Torbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the assignment of Mr. Torbica and Mr. Skondric? What were they supposed to do? You said that they came on behalf of the BiH MUP, from the Banja Luka area.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: In view of the fact that there was a disturbance of relations already and that the situation was complex, speaking ethnically, mixed checkpoints were to be set up on the territory covered by the Banja Luka centre, as well as the other centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could we please slow down. You mentioned mixed checkpoints. How do you mean, "mixed"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: It implies a mixed ethnic composition for the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Whose tasks were Mr. Skondric and Mr. Torbica carrying out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: They came on orders from the then Minister of the Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time who was Mr. Delimustafic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Vojin Bera, was he your superior?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: At one time he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As a long-term policeman, how did he carry out the assignments given him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: He was a very systematic man, very precise, carried out his assignments with precision, and always asked to have all the available information. He liked to check everything out mathematically, so that sometimes, at least when I was working there, if we made even any slight mathematical errors, he would make us repeat the task several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether the commission implemented its assignment from the head of the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I know that the commission went in the field, that it executed its tasks, and that a report was drawn up which was sent to the superiors, containing suggestions and proposals. The head of the State Security Service Centre, it was sent to the head of that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, this report, after it was reviewed by the State Security Service Centre, did the report result in anything? Did anything come of the report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Well, after the report was compiled, steps were taken to overcome the crisis situation and a decision was made to disband and disarm all paramilitary formations, that they should all come under legal institutions, that is to say, the regular army and its units and the regular police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who made the decision to disband all the paramilitary formations, and who said that it was only military units and regular police units who should be allowed to remain on the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: This decision was taken by the parliament, and the assembly decided that as of the 31st of August, up until that date, that all paramilitary units were to be disbanded and that anybody illegally in possession of arms was to relinquish those arms. That referred, in particular, to specific types of weapons, such as APCs, vehicles that people constructed themselves with special welding and armoured equipment and blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about the regular police institutions? During this period of time, that is to say, up until the 31st of August, 1992, did they encounter serious problems with these paramilitary formations and what they did on the ground, their actions on the ground? Did they encounter serious problems?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were big problems, major problems, because in the conditions that prevailed at the time, everything was unplanned and certain groups of individuals began to form with people of different profiles as members of these groups. Some joined the groups in order to ensure themselves a livelihood because -- and it was risky business. There was tension on all sides. Others were criminals, ordinary criminals with criminal records who wanted to use these units to further their own ends. So there were different motives. Some people were psychologically disturbed and did not have the mental capacity. So there were different types of people, and as the police, at that time, did not have enough trained men to deal with these people, because, as I say, some of the people in these groups had come in from other areas where combat was already under way and so they were better trained in the use of weapons, better trained than the police, and so very often the policemen didn't dare oppose such groups. So that was one of the reasons why it was proposed that this question be resolved on a state level, with the use of a coordinated action on the part of the army and the regular police force, that they should tackle the problem jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, does that mean that the police force had no control over these paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it did. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should now like to ask the witness to be shown document D38/1 that I brought up during my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. The question is: "Does that mean that the police force had no control over these paramilitary formations?" The answer says, "Yes, it did." It did have or it did not have? Can you say in a full sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: The police did not have any control, did not have full control over persons organised in a paramilitary fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, would you please take a look at this decision of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 14th of August, 1992. Is it the decision that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the signature of the head of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to turn to page 16.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: We have on that page the signatures of four individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, what about the English pagination? What page is it in the English text so that we can follow you? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking for the page number so that it can be placed on the ELMO. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] It is page 21 of the English text. Page 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do we have Vojin Bera listed as chairman under number 1?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I can say that Vojin Bera is the chairman. This is his signature as well as the signature of Jugoslav Rodic. As to the other two signatures, I know that Mr. Skondric was in the commission, but I can't identify and recognise his signature as I have never had occasion to see any official documents that he signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Jugoslav Rodic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and he has a very characteristic signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was he a member of the CSB of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the CSB of Banja Luka, the Prijedor department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You told me that you had occasion to see this report. You said that you knew the methods and characteristics of Mr. Bera. Do you consider that it is an analytical report of great precision with respect to the events that he was asked to investigate?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Because he's that kind of man is why he received the assignment, and probably the report -- had somebody else compiled the report, it might have been done in a fashion that was not as systematic as his.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija, you also see that there were attachments to this document whereby all the heads of the public security stations made reports for their own public security stations. Was that too one of the ways in which Mr. Bera worked, his method?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. It was always his method to have his subordinates do a part of the work and then to include their documents in the final document. And I'm talking about the time when he was my superior. That was his method of work. He would collect all the necessary data and information, compile it, and then sign it by way of authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In practice, did he check the data and information that the reports of his subordinates contained which he authorised and verified by placing his own signature to it.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That was his regular method of work. He loved finding any slips or errors made, and he ask for corrections if he found any mistakes, and he was very proud if he was able to find that somebody had slipped up on some point. He would make them revise their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: This report contains facts about the number of persons who were -- who went through the investigation centre. Was this report adopted?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the report was adopted and accepted as correct by the professional men of the centre, and on the basis of that document, the disbanding of the paramilitary formations was requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the report, he also states that in Omarska, 49 persons disappeared in ways that could not be explained. Now, when you hear the news that a bus carrying 49 people ran off the road, that would be the news of the day. Did this lead to an investigation of any kind? Do you know anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I think that one of the reasons for which these inspections were carried out was precisely to see what the actual state of affairs was because information had been received as to the misconduct of the military -- the paramilitary units and that the police was just not able to control these paramilitary units, and in that sense an investigation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If the Omarska camp -- or let me rephrase this. Knowing Mr. Bera as you did, who would you say he would be inclined to talk to about the investigations relative to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: He would talk to the competent people, the head of the public security station, but he would also make broader checks, and I suppose that he would involve also other people from the competent structures. That means he might have involved the deputy commander of the public security station. It was his method of work to consult the competent people, and I also believe he ran his own checks because he was that kind of man.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After the work of this commission and the activities it undertook, after this knowledge was obtained, was any action taken by Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: I believe there were -- there occurred situations which did not quite conform to the rules, and I believe that an interview was conducted with him, although I cannot discuss what was said there, but I don't believe there had been any serious discussions at the level of the centre, the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was this report forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I believe two copies of the report were forwarded, one to the state security sector, that means at the Ministry to the under-secretary for state security, and one to the under-secretary for public security who, naturally, presented it to the Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within your purview as liaison officer, did you at any time take any delegation to visit Omarska or Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SAMARDZIJA
utterances.text: No. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank this witness. I have no further questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thank him very much too. Mr. Krstan Simic, you said that you would work until 4.00 and you really did it. It's five to four. There is no point in us starting the cross-examination because we have only five minutes left, and in order not to interrupt the cross, we had better leave it until tomorrow. Mr. Samardzija, we will continue with you tomorrow at 9.20. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I am new to this Chamber, I would like to know, is it the Chamber's manner to inform the witness that there should be no discussion with anyone about the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We have made a decision on this. This decision stands and both parties are very well aware that after the witness has taken his oath, he cannot discuss his testimony with either party except in situations which must be notified to the Trial Chamber. Another exception we made were the accused and the expert witnesses. That is a different situation. But the witnesses we call normal, regular witnesses are not excepted from this rule. Since we have another two minutes left, I would like to say this: Each time when we are using documents -- we should resolve this matter. Mr. Simic, I believe I used your own documents, D38, I believe it was, and D39, which you will request be admitted into evidence. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, according to the method we used before for the cross-examination, and I suggest we do this immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but these documents were used in your opening statement. Ms. Somers, do you object to these documents 38 and 39? We are referring to the excerpts used by Mr. Simic in his opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe a good number of these documents are already admitted, perhaps under a different number. To the extent that that is the case, we would try to work with the registrar to get that straightened out because we also might want to make reference to some previously admitted documents, and as to anything that has just arisen, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation] It seems the court reporters can't hear me. I'm sorry. [In English] I shall speak English if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can the French interpreters and English interpreters check your buttons, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have done that. Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I believe that Ms. Somers already said that if, with regard to new documents, there are no objections -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Since I cannot communicate with Mr. Samardzija, I will have to ask the usher to take the document he has and have it copied for the benefit of the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right, but at the end of the testimony, nevertheless. So documents 38/1 and 39/1 are admitted into evidence. We'll continue tomorrow at 9.20. Thank you, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of January, 2001, at 9.20 a.m. 25
